newsitem.title: FRANCE: Nights of slaughter mark countdown to Algerian vote.
newsitem.headline: Nights of slaughter mark countdown to Algerian vote.

text.p: In the darkness surrounding two tiny Algerian communities overnight, suspected Moslem fundamentalists cut the throats of 18 people, Algerian security forces said on Thursday.
They reported the attacks in two brief statements within one hour of each other on the official Algerian news agency APS -- 11 people killed in Ain-Dema, seven in Douar Zemala.
The killings took place in Medea province south of Algiers, the eighth and ninth such attacks reported in two weeks, with three of them on consecutive nights.
They coincided with a stepped-up government campaign to get Algerians to turn out for a November 28 referendum to change the constitution.
"They (the Islamists) are trying to install a climate of fear in advance of the vote," one Western diplomat in Algiers said by telephone on Thursday.
But he added that the authorities could also be giving more publicity deliberately now to such attacks which they blame on Moslem fundamentalists.
One of the main changes in the proposed new constitution will be to ban political parties based on religion.

The fundamentalist Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) swept to a commanding lead in Algeria's last general election which the authorities cancelled in January 1992. The FIS was banned shortly afterwards amid widespread violence.
Referring to the attacks on villages, which have provoked anger, fear and demands by villagers for the authorities to arm them, the diplomat added:

"Incidents like these have been going on unreported but now they are reporting them. It is either connected with the referendum or the killings, near Algiers, are on such a scale that the authorities don't think they can cover them up.
"It is certainly becoming nastier," he said.
Algerian media are tightly censored on security issues, with the authorities releasing information in what another diplomat called "cycles", according to the message they want to give.
Few reports are carried on the deaths of members of the army or security forces.

On Thursday, Tangiers-based Mediterranee Internationale (Medi I) radio which beams across North Africa, quoting what it called a statement of the Islamic Salvation Army (AIS), said 48 people "including 10 soldiers and three militiamen have been killed" in recent days.
"These operations targeted the security forces and the so-called self-defence units," it quoted the AIS as saying.
The AIS is the military arm of the FIS. Most recent killings have been blamed on the more radical Armed Islamic Group (GIA), which broke from the FIS.
Another Western diplomat said the best evidence available suggested that between 150 and 200 people were being killed in Algeria each week.

With the most credible estimate of killings, put at a total of 50,000 in October last year by diplomats and Algeria's Human Rights Defence League, at least 60,000 people are now estimated to have died in the conflict.
Algeria's secular legal opposition puts the figure at 70,000 to 100,000 while the FIS, which recently condemned killing of civilians, says 120,000 have died.

Since last month, when President Liamine Zeroual announced the date of the referendum, there have been few reports of security forces killing rebels, for long the main feature of reports in the Algerian media on the five-year-old conflict.

Algiers-based diplomats say a big turnout is important to give credibility to the authorities' plan to change the constitution, and government ministers have for the past week been campaigning towards this.
Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia on Thursday exhorted residents of the eastern city of Constantine to turn out, while at least two cabinet ministers presided at similar meetings elsewhere.
